extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional comedy writers, sitcom staff writers, and stand-up comedians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft and career guidance for writing jokes, sitcom scripts, and stand-up material — emphasizing originality, theme, delivery, and writers' room norms. Advice is drawn from an experienced TV comedy writer's blog posts and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The rule of 2's
rubrics_metrics.description: On CHEERS we had the rule of 2’s. If the writing staff was working on a joke and any two writers pitched essentially the same punchline we automatically discarded it. Didn’t even matter if it was funny. Our feeling was that if two writers could come up with the same joke so could some audience members. And so it was quickly jettisoned. There was no debate. Ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two independent staffers arrive at the same punchline, consider it too obvious and remove it immediately — no argument. This is a staff-room filter for obviousness; the underlying rationale is that anything two professionals independently produce is likely predictable to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obvious / predictable punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: If I can predict a joke it’s just lazy writing. Either that or the staff is just not very good. When you’re trying to come up with a joke sometimes your first punchline might be the obvious one. Especially if you came up with it quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat initial, quick punchlines as suspects. Ask: is there a better joke? a fresher joke? something more unexpected or out in left field? Spend time digging beyond the first thought rather than accepting the quickest laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dig deeper for fresher and unexpected humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn to dig deeper. Is there a better joke? Is there a fresher joke? Is there something more unexpected? Maybe even something from out in leftfield?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively pursue surprises rather than settling for the obvious. The blog gives the practical prescription: don’t stop at the first idea — explore alternatives until you find the angle that’s less predictable and more surprising to an audience that has become sitcom-savvy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on catch-phrases or ironic shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-camera shows often resort to irony so it’s not even jokes. It’s catch-phrases or 'Gee, THAT went well.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t use tired catch-phrases, ironic asides, or shorthand punchlines as a substitute for real joke construction. These are easy and common, and they frequently feel lazy and predictable to today's audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for your show's genre and aim to be best in that lane
rubrics_metrics.description: Now I realize that not every show is CHEERS or is even going for the type of humor we went for. But you can strive to be the best in your genre, whatever it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the tone and aims of the show you're writing for and push to be the strongest exemplar of that style. Excellence is relative to genre — a Disney Channel sitcom can be superior within its category even if it’s different from an adult multi-camera comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make jokes that surprise and can still play over time
rubrics_metrics.description: If you watch a CHEERS today there will still be jokes that surprise you and make you laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for set pieces and punchlines with longevity — things that can still land for new viewers years later. Surprise and craftsmanship contribute to timelessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine theme before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing is I do is determine what the theme is before writing. The story, or in your case, album, should reflect that. Taking a finished product and sifting through it looking for gold is rather counter-productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the theme (the story's compass) early — preferably before drafting. This makes it easier to keep work on-track and to evaluate whether scenes or jokes serve the larger purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a unique comic persona and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: As a comic you can develop a persona that’s very unique to you. Their material is dependent as much on delivery and character as the written words themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a distinctive voice/character and delivery style; this makes material harder to steal and more identifiable. Examples cited: Woody Allen, Richard Pryor, Steve Martin, Mitch Hedberg — performers whose persona is integral to the humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry norm on joke ownership: first public performance matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If there’s a question of ownership over a particular joke, the comic that delivered it on TV first gets it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that informal industry practice awards priority to the first high-profile performance (especially TV). This is an informal standard rather than a legal one, and can disadvantage lesser-known comics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical enforcement against joke stealing (non-legal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics tend to ostracize other comics who steal material. The problem gets handled by ostracism, blackballing by clubs, public exposure, and the informal comedians' code; legal action is usually impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because copyright litigation is expensive and unreliable for individual jokes, the scene depends on social enforcement (calling out plagiarists, club blacklists). Maintain dated records (videos, tweets) to document origination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal recourse for joke theft is generally impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: If you sue for copyright infringement it’ll cost all parties involved anywhere from $373,000 to $2.1 million. It better be one fucking great joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't expect the courts to be a practical remedy for most joke theft disputes; plan career and personal strategies (documentation, exposure control, unique delivery) rather than litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff work requires the temperament to handle pressure and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: When people tell me they just want to start writing and see where the story takes them, I tell them most often it leads to Death Valley. Put in the time and effort to determine your theme first. There are a lot of terrific comedy writers who just don’t have the temperament for staff work. You may get a supportive room; you may not. It depends on the personalities in the room, the pressure they’re all under...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a writers' room is high-pressure and often abrasive; you need thick skin and the ability to produce consistently. If you’re sensitive or prone to depression, consider alternatives (freelance writing, screenplays, stage plays) or focus on producing great drafts so you can work outside the room system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish strong drafts to advance your career (freelance/screenplay options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time was you could make a living in TV as a freelance writer. No more really. But if you write great drafts you may get a show to give you multiple assignments. And a better avenue might be to write screenplays. Or stage plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bulk staff work isn't right for you, invest in producing strong, finished drafts (spec scripts, screenplays, stage plays) that can open other career paths.
